_note: Study notes keyed to the VAPT syllabus (CY255TBD). 'source' lists the textbook chapter and section headings (verified against the PDF outlines supplied); summaries are paraphrased explanations, not quotations. PRAWL does not perform exploitation.

concepts.title: Social engineering
concepts.summary: Attacks on people instead of software: phishing (fake e-mails/sites), pretexting (invented story), baiting (infected USB / free download), tailgating (following someone through a door). A pen-tester follows the same steps as an attacker: research the target, build a believable pretext, make contact, then measure who clicks, replies or hands over access. Defences are awareness training, verification procedures and technical controls.
concepts.prawl_link: PRAWL checks the technical defences: SPF/DMARC (stops forged mail from your domain) and a look-alike domain watch (typosquats used for phishing).

source.sections: How a Social Engineering Attack Works; Conducting a Social Engineering Attack; Defending Against Social Engineering Attacks

concepts.title: Information gathering (reconnaissance)
concepts.summary: The first technical phase of a test: learn the target without touching it harshly. Passive sources: DNS, certificate-transparency logs, WHOIS, search engines, public code. Active: banner grabbing, port scanning. Everything later depends on this map of hosts, software and versions.
concepts.prawl_link: PRAWL reads DNS records, the TLS certificate, HTTP banners and robots.txt; the advanced scan lists subdomains from crt.sh certificate-transparency logs.

concepts.title: Physical penetration & insider attacks
concepts.summary: Testing whether someone can walk into a building, plug a device into the network or clone an access badge. Common ways in: tailgating, unattended server rooms, unlocked workstations, dumpster diving. Insiders already have access, so defences are least privilege, separation of duties, logging and prompt de-provisioning.
concepts.prawl_link: Not testable from the internet, so PRAWL lists it as out of scope instead of guessing. Access-control gaps that matter for insiders are mapped to the DPDP 'restrict access' obligation.

source.chapter: Ch. 5 Physical Penetration Attacks and Ch. 6 Insider Attacks
source.sections: Why a Physical Penetration Is Important; Common Ways into a Building; Defending Against Insider Attacks

concepts.title: Metasploit framework & Meterpreter
concepts.summary: A framework that organises exploits, payloads, auxiliary scanners and post-exploitation modules. Typical flow: pick a module, set RHOSTS/LHOST, choose a payload, run. Meterpreter is an in-memory payload offering a shell, file transfer, pivoting and credential dumping. Resource scripts automate repeatable sequences.
concepts.prawl_link: PRAWL never runs exploits. It does flag CVEs that are on the CISA Known Exploited list, which are the ones attackers already weaponise.

source.sections: Using the Metasploit Console to Launch Exploits; Penetration Testing with Metasploit's Meterpreter; Automating and Scripting Metasploit

concepts.title: Planning, executing and reporting a penetration test
concepts.summary: Planning fixes the scope (what is in/out), the rules of engagement (hours, allowed techniques, emergency contact) and written authorisation. Execution follows information gathering, vulnerability analysis, exploitation and post-exploitation. Information sharing keeps the client informed during the test. The report has an executive summary, technical findings with evidence, risk ratings and prioritised remediation.
concepts.prawl_link: Each scan shows its scope, rules of engagement, which phases ran and which did not, plus a prioritised remediation plan.

concepts.title: Stack operations & buffer overflows
concepts.summary: Each function call pushes a stack frame: arguments, the saved return address and local buffers. Writing past the end of a local buffer (e.g. unchecked strcpy) overwrites the saved return address; when the function returns, the CPU jumps where the attacker chose. Local buffer-overflow exploits use this to run shellcode or to reuse existing code (return-to-libc, ROP). Fixes: bounds-checked APIs, stack canaries, DEP/NX, ASLR, memory-safe languages.
concepts.prawl_link: A web scan cannot see memory bugs, but outdated server software is where they live, so PRAWL matches disclosed versions against recent CVEs (several October 2026 critical entries are memory-corruption flaws).

source.sections: Stack Operations; Buffer Overflows; Local Buffer Overflow Exploits

concepts.title: Exploit development process (Linux)
concepts.summary: Typical order: 1) find the crash (fuzzing), 2) confirm control of the instruction pointer, 3) find the exact offset, 4) identify bad characters, 5) pick a return target, 6) add a payload, 7) test and harden against protections. Tools: gdb, pattern generators, objdump. Always done in a lab on your own systems.
concepts.prawl_link: Out of scope for PRAWL (a non-destructive scanner). Understanding the process explains why patching promptly matters.

concepts.title: Windows exploits: SEH and memory protections
concepts.summary: Structured Exception Handling (SEH) stores a chain of handlers on the stack; overwriting a handler record lets an attacker take control when an exception occurs. Windows defences: /GS stack cookies, SafeSEH and SEHOP (validate the handler chain), DEP (non-executable data pages), ASLR (randomised addresses). Older platforms (XP SP3, Vista, Server 2008) enforce these differently, which is why bypass techniques are version-specific.
concepts.prawl_link: PRAWL flags exposed Windows services such as RDP and outdated IIS/ASP.NET banners; the binary-level protections themselves need a debugger, not a remote scanner.

source.sections: Understanding Structured Exception Handling (SEH); Understanding Windows Memory Protections (XP SP3, Vista, 7, and Server 2008); Bypassing Windows Memory Protections

concepts.title: OWASP Top 10 web application risks
concepts.summary: A consensus list of the most critical web risks (2021 edition): Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration, Vulnerable and Outdated Components, Identification and Authentication Failures, Software and Data Integrity Failures, Logging and Monitoring Failures, SSRF.
concepts.prawl_link: Every PRAWL finding is tagged with its OWASP category and CWE id, and the report shows which categories were assessed versus not assessed.

source.sections: Overview of Top Web Application Security Vulnerabilities (the 2021 category list itself is from owasp.org)

concepts.title: Injection (SQL injection)
concepts.summary: Untrusted input is concatenated into a query or command, so data becomes code. Classic payload: ' OR '1'='1. Variants: error-based, union-based, blind boolean/time-based. Fix with parameterised queries / prepared statements, least-privilege database accounts and input validation.
concepts.prawl_link: The optional advanced scan runs SQLMap (with consent). A confirmed SQL injection opens a direct path to customer data in the attack-path graph.

concepts.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
concepts.summary: Attacker-controlled script runs in a victim's browser: reflected (in the request), stored (saved by the site) or DOM-based. Impact: session theft, defacement, actions as the user. Fix by encoding output for its context, using HttpOnly cookies and a strict Content-Security-Policy.
concepts.prawl_link: PRAWL sends a harmless marker containing HTML characters and reports it only if it comes back unencoded. A missing CSP alone is NOT treated as an XSS vulnerability.

concepts.title: Vulnerability analysis: passive, source-code and binary
concepts.summary: Passive analysis observes normal traffic and responses without attacking (headers, cookies, comments, versions). Source-code analysis reads code or served HTML/JS for dangerous patterns. Binary analysis inspects compiled programs (disassembly, fuzzing) when source is unavailable.
concepts.prawl_link: Passive: header, cookie, banner and TLS checks. Source analysis: landing-page HTML (mixed content, forms, comments). Binary analysis is not applicable to a hosted website.

concepts.title: Client-side browser exploits
concepts.summary: Instead of attacking a server, the attacker lures a user to a page that exploits their browser or a plug-in: use-after-free, type confusion, and heap spraying (filling the heap with shellcode so a corrupted pointer lands on it). Protections: automatic updates, sandboxing, site isolation, DEP/ASLR, and CSP on your own site so it cannot be turned into a delivery vehicle.
concepts.prawl_link: PRAWL checks your CSP/XFO headers and third-party script integrity, the controls that stop your site from serving client-side attacks.

source.sections: Heap Spray to Exploit; Protecting Yourself from Client-Side Exploits

concepts.title: Malware analysis & honeypots
concepts.summary: Honeypots are decoy systems that record attacker behaviour and capture malware samples (low-interaction ones emulate services; high-interaction ones are real systems). Collected samples get initial analysis: static (hashes, strings, imports, packers) then dynamic (run in a sandbox and watch files, registry, network).
concepts.prawl_link: Beyond an external scanner. PRAWL's look-alike domain watch applies the same idea defensively: it finds fake copies of your domain before customers do.
